records.title: E63/E64 Active Steering and Steering-Gear Play / Knock
records.description: On the E63/E64 6 Series and M6, owners report knocking and developing play from the steering gear (Lenkgetriebe), often associated with the Active Steering setup. German forums (motor-talk.de) describe a clacking/knocking noise and light play in the steering, with replacement steering gears quoted at well over 3,000 euros plus installation. Alongside the steering gear, the front control-arm bushings and other rubber suspension bearings wear out around 150,000-200,000 km, contributing to clunks and loose steering feel.
records.solution: Inspect the steering gear and front control-arm/thrust-arm bushings for play. Replace worn control-arm bushings/ball joints first as they are cheaper and frequently the source of the knock; if the steering rack/gear itself has internal play or leaks, it requires replacement (a significant cost) followed by an alignment.
symptoms: Knocking/clacking from the steering when turning or over bumps
Light play / vagueness in the steering
Clunk from the front suspension
Uneven front tire wear

records.title: F12 Convertible Top Hydraulic Pump and Relay Failure
records.description: On the F12 M6 Convertible, the soft-top is operated by a hydraulic pump unit. Owners (including on German forums such as motor-talk.de) report the top stops opening or closing mid-cycle, operates slowly or jams. The most common root causes are the two high-current relays in the hydraulic pump unit sticking/failing and the pump itself losing pressure over time; hydraulic fluid leaks and sensor faults also occur. The relays are inexpensive but the pump rebuild/replacement is costly, and a stuck top can leave the car undriveable in the rain.
records.solution: Diagnose whether the fault is the pump's high-current relays (relatively cheap, often the cure), a pressure loss in the pump, a hydraulic leak, or a roof microswitch/sensor. Replace the relays first; if pressure loss persists, rebuild or replace the hydraulic pump unit (specialist rebuild services exist) and renew worn seals/sensors. Bleed and refill the hydraulic system after repair.
symptoms: Convertible top stops part-way through opening or closing
Slow or inconsistent top operation
Top jams or fails to move
Hydraulic fluid leak near the pump unit
Roof error message in the cluster

records.title: F12/F13 7-Speed M-DCT Mechatronic and Clutch Pack Failure
records.description: The F06/F12/F13 M6 uses a 7-speed M dual-clutch transmission (GS7D36/GS7D70). Owners report two main problems: failure of the mechatronic unit (the DCT's electronic/hydraulic control module), which causes erratic shifting, stored transmission fault codes and limp/failsafe mode; and premature clutch-pack wear, which causes slipping, harsh or jerky engagement and a burning smell, particularly in stop-and-go driving or on tuned cars. This is a separate transmission from the SMG used on the earlier V10 M6.
records.solution: Scan for transmission codes to confirm whether the fault is the mechatronic unit or worn clutch packs. Mechatronic units can often be repaired/replaced and must be reprogrammed and adapted to the vehicle afterward. Worn clutch packs require a clutch replacement (dealer cost often $3,000-$5,000). Regular DCT fluid and filter changes help prevent premature wear; avoid prolonged clutch slip in traffic.
symptoms: Erratic or harsh shifting
Transmission warning light / failsafe (limp) mode
Clutch slipping or hesitation engaging gears
Jerking in stop-and-go traffic
Burning smell from the transmission area

records.title: F12/F13 Electric Water Pump and Thermostat Failure
records.description: The F06/F12/F13 M6 with the S63 twin-turbo V8 uses an electrically driven coolant pump and an electronic thermostat. Both are common failure points. The electric water pump can fail electronically (no flow) and the thermostat can stick, while cracked radiator end-tanks and a leaking expansion tank are also reported. Because the twin-turbo V8 generates significant under-bonnet heat, cooling-system failures can quickly lead to overheating and, if ignored, head-gasket or bearing damage. This affects the M6 specifically and is separate from the engine-bearing and turbo issues.
records.solution: Replace the failed electric water pump and/or electronic thermostat with OEM units; inspect the radiator end-tanks and expansion tank for cracks and replace as needed. Pressure-test the cooling system, refresh coolant, and treat the pump/thermostat as wear items given the heat load. Address any overheating event immediately to avoid secondary engine damage.
symptoms: Rising coolant temperature / overheating warning
Rapid coolant loss
Coolant smell or visible leak under the car
Engine running hot in traffic
Low coolant level warning

records.title: F12/F13 Turbocharger Wastegate Rattle and Oil Starvation
records.description: The S63 twin-turbo V8 in the F06/F12/F13 M6 is prone to wastegate rattle as the wastegate actuator linkage develops play with heat cycling, producing a metallic rattle at light throttle/low load. The turbos can also suffer oil-feed coking/starvation due to the intense under-bonnet heat (a hot-V layout with turbos in the engine valley), leading to bearing wear, whining, power loss and increased turbo lag if neglected. Heat management and clean oil are central to turbo longevity on this engine.
records.solution: Confirm wastegate rattle by listening at light throttle; worn actuators/linkages can be replaced or upgraded. For oil starvation, maintain strict oil-change intervals with the correct specification, allow proper cool-down after hard driving, and keep the cooling system healthy. Severely worn or whining turbos require rebuild or replacement.
symptoms: Metallic rattle at light throttle / low load
Turbo whine or whistle
Power loss and increased turbo lag
Excessive exhaust smoke in severe cases

records.title: Rod Bearing Premature Wear (S65/S63 Engines)
records.description: Both the S65 V8 (E63 M6) and S63 twin-turbo V8 (F06/F12/F13 M6) suffer from premature rod bearing wear. The S65 is particularly notorious — the OEM rod bearings use a copper-lead composition that wears rapidly, especially with frequent cold starts and short trips. The S63 has improved bearings but can still experience wear at higher mileages. Failure to catch worn bearings leads to spun bearings and catastrophic engine failure.
records.solution: Perform a preventive rod bearing replacement between 60,000-80,000 miles on S65 engines, and inspect by 80,000-100,000 miles on S63 engines. Use upgraded ACL or King XP bearings with coated surfaces. Cut and send used oil filter for analysis — bearing material particles indicate wear progression. The job requires engine-out on the S65 (approximately 20 hours labor) or can be done in-car on the S63 with the oil pan dropped.
symptoms: Metallic ticking or knocking from engine at idle
Copper or bronze particles visible in oil filter
Oil analysis showing elevated copper and lead levels
Roughness felt through drivetrain at low RPM
Engine knock under load

communityRecommendations.text: Do NOT wait for symptoms — by the time you hear knocking, damage is already done. Preventive replacement at 60k is cheap insurance on a $15k+ engine.

records.title: S63 Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves (Direct Injection)
records.description: The S63 twin-turbo V8 in the F06/F12/F13 M6 uses direct fuel injection, so no fuel washes over the back of the intake valves. Over time, oil vapor from the crankcase ventilation system bakes onto the intake valves and ports, restricting airflow. This produces rough idle, cold-start stumble, misfires and a loss of low-end response, typically becoming noticeable from roughly 50,000-70,000 km onward. It is a normal direct-injection characteristic rather than a defect, but it is widely reported by M6 owners and requires periodic service.
records.solution: Have the intake valves walnut-blasted (media-blast cleaning) to remove carbon deposits without removing the cylinder heads. Many owners do this every 50,000-70,000 km. A properly functioning PCV/crankcase ventilation system and quality oil reduce deposit rate. An oil-catch can is sometimes fitted to slow accumulation.
symptoms: Rough idle
Cold-start stumble / hesitation
Misfires under load
Loss of low-end power and throttle response
Reduced fuel economy

records.title: S63 High-Pressure Fuel Pump / Fuel Injector Cold-Start Misfire
records.description: The S63/N63 V8 family used in the F12/F13 M6 is subject to high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) and direct-injector problems. A failing HPFP causes long cranking and hard starting (worst when cold), rough running and misfires from insufficient rail pressure. Separately, the direct injectors can develop internal leaks, dumping excess fuel and causing cold-start rough running, misfires and a Service Engine light. BMW issued a service bulletin for N63/S63 engines in F12/F13 addressing rough cold-start running with illuminated service lights traced to internal high-pressure injector failure; injectors must be matched to the correct index per bank.
records.solution: Scan for misfire and fuel-system codes and test cold-start fuel-rail pressure. Replace a failing HPFP; for injector faults, replace the affected injector(s) with units of the correct matching index code (do not mix injector indexes on a bank) and re-code them. Address per the relevant BMW technical service bulletin for the N63/S63.
symptoms: Long crank / hard starting, worst when cold
Rough running and misfires after a cold start
Hesitation or stumble during acceleration
Check Engine / Service Engine Soon light
Reduced fuel economy

records.title: S63 Twin-Turbo V8 Rod Bearing Concerns (F06/F12/F13 M6)
records.description: The S63 4.4L twin-turbo V8 engine in the F06/F12/F13 M6 (2013-2018) has rod bearing concerns similar to but less catastrophic than the S85 V10. While the S63 bearing clearances are better than the notoriously tight S85, bearings can still wear prematurely under hard driving or track use, especially at high mileage. Bearing wear is accelerated by BMW's recommended 10,000-mile oil change intervals (too long for this engine). Preventive rod bearing replacement is recommended at 60,000-80,000 miles for peace of mind, particularly for cars that see track days or spirited driving. Oil changes every 5,000-7,500 miles are mandatory to extend bearing life. ACL Race Rod Bearings 8B1578HX-STD ($150-250) or King Bearings SV Series are the community-recommended upgrades over OEM. WPC-treated bearings from Lang Racing offer the best durability for track use.
records.solution: Preventive rod bearing replacement at 60,000-80,000 miles using ACL Race Rod Bearings 8B1578HX-STD ($150-250), King Bearings SV Series, or WPC-treated bearings from Lang Racing. Cost: $4,000-7,000 for preventive replacement. Oil changes every 5,000-7,500 miles mandatory (ignore BMW's 10,000-mile recommendation). Use Blackstone Labs oil analysis ($30/test) every 5,000 miles to monitor bearing wear metals. Preventive replacement recommended for peace of mind, especially on cars used for track days or spirited driving.
symptoms: Faint ticking or knocking noise from bottom end (early wear)
Elevated copper/lead levels in oil analysis
Oil pressure drop at idle when engine is hot
Metal particles on magnetic drain plug
Engine knocking under load (advanced wear)
Catastrophic engine failure (if bearings spin)

records.title: S85 V10 Rod Bearing Failure (Catastrophic Engine Destruction)
records.description: The S85 5.0L V10 engine in the E63 M6 (2006-2010) has catastrophically tight rod bearing clearances (0.001" vs 0.0025" industry standard) with thin OEM bearings that fail prematurely, leading to spun bearings and complete engine destruction. This is the single most critical issue on any BMW M car. OEM bearings are inadequate - they WILL fail, typically between 60,000-100,000 miles, often sooner with track use. Failure modes include sudden loss of oil pressure, knocking, and seized engine. Blackstone Labs oil analysis every 5,000 miles ($30/test) is mandatory to monitor bearing wear metals (copper, lead, tin). If copper levels spike above 30 PPM, bearings are failing and must be replaced immediately. NEVER use OEM bearings as replacements - use ACL Race Bearings with +0.001" extra clearance. Bimmerpost/M5Board consensus: this is MANDATORY preventive maintenance before 70,000 miles.
records.solution: MANDATORY PREVENTIVE REPLACEMENT before 70,000 miles: Replace all 10 rod bearings with ACL Race Bearings 10B1580HX-STD (+0.001" clearance, $200-350) or WPC-treated bearings from Lang Racing, or VAC Motorsports kit VAC-HPRBK-S85, or Turner kit TMS222798, or FCP Euro kit 11247841703KT3. ALSO replace VANOS line 11367838669 and use ARP rod bolts (included in most kits). Cost: $6,500-9,500 preventive. If engine is destroyed from bearing failure: $15,000-32,000 for engine replacement or rebuild. NEVER use OEM bearings as replacements. Use Blackstone Labs oil analysis every 5,000 miles ($30/test) to monitor bearing wear metals.
symptoms: Engine knocking or ticking noise (bearing wear)
Sudden loss of oil pressure (bearing failure in progress)
Metal particles in oil or on magnetic drain plug
Elevated copper/lead/tin in Blackstone Labs oil analysis
Engine seizure (catastrophic failure)
Oil pressure warning light

records.title: S85 V10 Throttle Actuator Failure (Plastic Gear Stripping)
records.description: The S85 V10 engine in the E63 M6 (2006-2010) uses individual throttle bodies with internal throttle actuators containing plastic PPA (polyphthalamide) gears that strip over time, typically around 70,000 miles. The plastic gear teeth are gradually worn down by the metal worm drive, causing the throttle body to lose position control. When the gears strip, the affected bank of cylinders loses throttle control, causing limp mode, rough running, and diagnostic codes 2B15 or 2B16 (throttle actuator faults). The S85 has 2 throttle actuators (one per bank of 5 cylinders) - both should be rebuilt at the same time. Beisan Systems sintered metal replacement gears are the permanent fix - they outlast the plastic OEM gears indefinitely. This is a well-documented issue on M5Board and Bimmerpost.
records.solution: Rebuild throttle actuators using Beisan Systems BS101 sintered metal gear kit ($250/set, need 2 sets for both actuators) for permanent fix. Beisan BS102 full rebuild service available ($300). Alternatively, rebuilt actuators from Euro Power Motorsports ($500-800 each). OEM replacement actuators from BMW cost $2,000-4,500. Total cost: $500-4,500 depending on approach. Beisan Systems sintered metal gears are THE permanent fix - they replace the weak plastic PPA gears with metal gears that will not strip. Always rebuild both actuators simultaneously.
symptoms: Check engine light with codes 2B15 or 2B16 (throttle actuator fault)
Limp mode / reduced power mode
Rough idle or engine running on fewer cylinders
Throttle response becomes erratic or delayed
Engine hesitation on acceleration
One bank of cylinders not responding to throttle input

records.title: S85 V10 VANOS High-Pressure Oil Pump Failure
records.description: On the S85 5.0L V10 (E63/E64 M6), the VANOS variable-valve-timing system runs off a dedicated high-pressure oil pump mounted in the oil pan that must produce roughly 1,000 psi. Over time the pump's internal seals wear and the high-pressure VANOS lines can split, causing pressure to drop dramatically (owners have measured as low as ~180 psi against the ~1,000 psi spec). The pump can eventually disintegrate, contaminating the engine with debris. This is a distinct failure from rod-bearing wear and is one of the most expensive non-bearing repairs on the V10. Left unaddressed it can cause valvetrain and broader engine damage.
records.solution: Perform an oil-pressure test on the VANOS circuit at the first sign of cold-start knocking. Replace or professionally rebuild the high-pressure VANOS pump and renew the high-pressure lines/seals. Many owners do the VANOS pump preventively at the same time as the rod-bearing service since the oil pan is already removed. Use only BMW-spec oil and strict change intervals to prolong pump life.
symptoms: Knocking/rattling noise from the cam hubs while cranking
Gentle knocking from the front of the cylinder heads while running
Jerky power delivery at low RPM
Loss of high-RPM performance / rough running
VANOS fault codes / Check Engine Light

records.title: SMG Hydraulic Pump and Clutch Actuator Failure
records.description: The E63/E64 M6 uses a Sequential Manual Gearbox (SMG III) that relies on a hydraulic pump and actuator to operate the clutch. The SMG pump is prone to failure, typically between 60,000 and 90,000 miles. When the pump fails, the car displays "SMG Transmission Fault" and may become undrivable. The hydraulic accumulator (pressure sphere) also loses its charge over time, causing slow or jerky shifts before complete failure.
records.solution: Replace the SMG hydraulic pump and pressure accumulator. Bleed and refill the SMG hydraulic system with Pentosin CHF 11S fluid. Many owners convert to a traditional 6-speed manual swap using an aftermarket kit from companies like OS Giken or using the E90 M3 6MT parts. Budget $2,000-4,000 for SMG repair or $5,000-8,000 for a manual conversion.
symptoms: SMG Transmission Fault warning on iDrive
Slow or jerky gear changes
Grinding noise during gear engagement
Car stuck in gear or unable to select gear
Hydraulic pump running constantly
